newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-OPEC helped by scarcer other oil supply-IEA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OPEC helped by scarcer other oil supply-IEA.

text.p: Supplies from non-OPEC producers will not hit the heights previously expected in the fourth quarter while demand will be higher, leaving extra room for OPEC crude oil on world markets, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Tuesday.

Global demand in the fourth quarter is now projected at a record 73.7 million barrels a day (bpd), a 100,000 bpd upward revision on last month's estimate, the Paris-based energy watchdog said in its monthly oil market report.
Year-on-year, the world's thirst for oil is expected to grow a sharp 1.7 million bpd in 1996 and a further 1.8 million bpd in 1997.

But some analysts say that the IEA projections may be conservative. A robust United States economy and runaway demand in several large consumers like India, South Korea and Brazil could boost global oil use even more.
"We think the IEA will have to make further upward revisions to demand as the year goes on," said Mehdi Varzi, an oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

Varzi and others also think the agency is overestimating its non-OPEC supply figures. On Tuesday, the agency revised down its previous estimate for fourth quarter output from producers outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Counties (OPEC) by 200,000 bpd to 45.0 million bpd.
But that is still a whopping 1.5 million rise over the third quarter and an even more impressive 2.3 million over fourth quarter 1995.
Demand for OPEC oil and stocks in the fourth quarter has been boosted by 300,000 bpd to 25.9 million bpd, close to current production of about 25.88 million bpd.

The surge in demand combined with Middle East tensions, the non-OPEC supply shortfalls, a delay in the return of Iraqi oil exports and pre-winter heating oil stockpiling has boosted oil prices to post-Gulf War highs and given OPEC a $20-$25 billion oil revenue windfall this year.
"You could say luck has been on our side this year," one OPEC official said.
Though OPEC production is well above its 25.03 million bpd ceiling as most OPEC members pump more than their allotted quotas, it could hardly be called overproduction, analysts say.
Consumers lap up every available barrel and inventories in both Europe and the United States remain at worryingly low levels ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.

"OPEC has been overproducing for a long time but this only becomes a problem when demand is lower than supply. Now that is not a problem," said Bo Van Wijk, vice-president of energy risk management at UBS bank.
But OPEC is unlikely to rush to cash in on the revenue bonanza and the higher demand forecast by increasing its ceiling when it meets in November to set 1997 levels, OPEC delegates and analysts say.

"They are getting so much more revenue at the moment. They do not want to jeopardise that by having an open row about quotas because it could destabilise the market," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES).
Just a few months ago, analysts were predicting the beginning of the end of OPEC when ministers in June failed to cut production to make room for Iraq.

But the United Nations' plan to allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to pay for food and medicines is on hold after Baghdad's attack of two Kurdish strongholds in Western-protected northern Iraq.
Now analysts ask whether the world can meet demand if there is a repeat of last winter's frigid temperatures.
"No one can avoid a price spike if the weather is cold. Somewhere all the oil is disappearing," said UBS' Van Wijk.
